en: The Praise of the Dharmakāya as Requested by Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva from the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* in One Hundred Thousand Verses.
By the Duke of Sū, Minister of State, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, and Special Advancement.

Feudal estate of three thousand households; conferred the purple robe and the title of Minister of Works; posthumous name: Dajian (Great Mirror); the Tripitaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daguangzhi Daxingshan Monastery, by imperial decree, translates: I take refuge and pay homage to the Dharmakāya, which dwells within all sentient beings;
because they do not fully know it, they transmigrate through the three realms of existence.
Its nature is birth and death, and it is likewise so when pure;
this purity is nirvāṇa, and it is also the dharmakāya.
It is like milk and cream mixed together, wherein the clarified butter (sarpis) cannot be found.
Just as when mixed with afflictions, the dharma-realm cannot be seen;
just as when pure milk has been processed, the essence of ghee is wondrous and stainless;
so too, when its afflictions are purified, the dharma-realm is utterly pure.
Just as a lamp within its jar has no radiance, so too,
when within the jar of afflictions, the dharma-realm does not shine.
By making an opening in that very jar, it allows light to emerge from one side.
From each and every side, light radiates outward.
With the vajra of samādhi, one shatters the jar of afflictions;
it fills the entirety of space, shining with universal brilliance.
The Dharma-realm is neither born nor ever destroyed;
at all times it is unstained, pure from beginning to end and always without blemish.
Like vaidūrya, it is perpetually and intensely luminous.
Just as when covered by a stone treasury, that light does not shine forth;
so too, when obscured by afflictions, the wondrously pure dharmadhātu does not illuminate saṃsāra, nor does its radiance shine upon nirvāṇa.
If one possesses the potential and applies effort, then the true gold will be revealed;
if one lacks the potential despite applying effort, one will be exhausted without any gain.
Just as rice covered by its husk is not called *śāli* grain;
When covered by afflictions, it is not called the Buddha;
Just as when freed from the husk, the grain reveals itself;
So too, when separated from afflictions, The Dharma-body is made manifest.
The world employs this analogy: the plantain tree has no core of solidity;
yet it bears firm and substantial fruit, whose flavor is like nectar.
So too, though birth and death lack any true reality, one wanders through the ocean of afflictions.
That fruit is the very body of the Buddha; it bestows the nectar of immortality upon those who give.
Thus, from various seeds, fruits of a corresponding nature arise;
that there could be no fruit without a seed—this the wise would certainly not believe.
The seed is its very nature, the basis upon which all phenomena depend;
if this can be purified through successive stages, one attains the state of Buddhahood.
The sun and moon are eternally stainless, yet they are obscured by five kinds of veils:
Just as clouds, mist, smoke, The hand of Rāhu, and dust,
So does the radiance of the mind Become obscured by the five defilements:
Covetousness, ill-will, sloth, Agitation, and doubt.
Just as when one washes a garment with fire, though it is defiled by various impurities,
if it is cast into the flames, the filth is burned away but the garment is not.
All the sūtras of the same category as emptiness were spoken by the Tathāgata.
All afflictions are severed, yet their nature is never destroyed.
Just as subterranean water remains eternally pure,
so too is wisdom hidden within afflictions— its purity likewise remains unchanged.
The dharma-realm is neither self, nor female, nor male;
being far removed from all attachments, how could one discriminate a self?
All phenomena are without clinging, for "female" and "male" cannot be apprehended.
Because they have subdued the blindness of craving, they manifest in the forms of men and women.
Impermanence, suffering, and emptiness—these are the three aspects of pure mental application;
the most supreme pure mental application is that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
Just as a child conceived in the womb exists yet is not manifest,
so too, when obscured by afflictions, the reality of phenomena cannot be seen.
There are four kinds of conceptualization regarding that which is produced from the great elements:
Discriminating between self and what belongs to self, Names, concepts, and their objects—
All the great vows of the Buddhas Are non-existent and signless;
Because they correspond to self-awakening, The Buddhas are eternally the Dharma-nature.
Just as one speaks of a rabbit having horns, which exist only through conceptual construction and not in reality;
so it is with all phenomena, which cannot be found through conceptualization.
Even when analyzed down to the level of subtle atoms, they cannot be found through conceptualization.
As it was in the beginning, so it is at the end; how can wisdom make such distinctions?
Thus, that which arises through combination also perishes through combination;
since not a single dharma arises of itself, why do the deluded make such distinctions?
The analogy of the two horns of a rabbit and an ox is called the characteristic of pervasive conceptualization;
abiding therein in the Middle Way is like the dharmatā of the Sugata.
Like the moon and the stars appearing in a vessel of clear water, [so does the nature of reality manifest].
Appearing as reflections, such is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*).
Good in the beginning and the middle, it is eternal and never deceptive;
since it lacks the five kinds of self (*ātman*), how can there be conceptualization of a self?
Just as water when hot is called "hot water," and when it is cold is called "cold water," so too that which is covered by the net of afflictions is called "mind."
If one is free from those afflictions, Then one is called "Equal Enlightenment.
When visual consciousness takes form as its object, The reflected image is utterly pure;
Neither arising nor ceasing, The Dharma-realm is without form or characteristic.
The ear-consciousness takes sound as its object; these three kinds of pure consciousnesses hear through their own discrimination, yet the dharma-realm is without form or characteristic.
The nose smells based on fragrance; it is neither color nor shape.
Olfactory consciousness is suchness; the dharma-realm should be discerned.
The nature of the tongue-element is empty; the nature of the taste-element is remote.
There is no support and no consciousness, because this is the self-nature of the dharma-realm.
The pure self-nature of the body, The characteristic of the harmony of what is touched;
Detached from all objects of perception— This I call the dharmadhātu.
Of all phenomena, the mind is supreme; It is free from the discrimination of subject and object.
The dharma-realm has no intrinsic nature, yet the dharma-realm is conceptually differentiated.
That which can see, hear, and smell, as well as taste and what is touched—this is known through the method of yoga;
such is the characteristic of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*).
The eye, ear, and nose, the tongue, body, and the mental faculty—
when these six sense bases are all pure, such is their characteristic.
The mind-seeing is of two kinds:
mundane and supramundane;
grasping at a self constitutes saṃsāra, while self-awakening is suchness (tathatā).
The inexhaustible is nirvāṇa; when greed and delusion are exhausted, awakening to that as the essence of the Buddha is the place where sentient beings take refuge.
Within this very body, whether one possesses wisdom or lacks it—
Bound by one's own conceptual constructions, one attains liberation through awakening.
Awakening is neither near nor far; it neither comes nor goes.
Within this web of afflictions, there is both destruction and manifestation.
Expounding upon the various sūtras, Abiding in self-reflection;
Illuminating with the lamp of wisdom, One immediately attains supreme tranquility.
There is no thought that awakening is distant, Nor is there any thought that it is near.
These images of the six objects are all known through such understanding:
Like water and milk mixed together within a single vessel,
A goose drinks up all the milk, While the water remains as it was before.
Thus, while mixed with afflictions, wisdom resides within a single vessel;
the yogin drinks the wisdom and abandons the afflictions.
In this way, from the notion of "I" and the grasping at a self, up to the grasping at objects of perception;
If one perceives the two kinds of selflessness, the seeds of existence are destroyed.
This is the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha—eternal, constant, pure, and stainless.
Fools engage in dualistic discrimination; it is the non-dual state of yoga.
Various difficult acts of giving, gathering sentient beings through ethical discipline,
and enduring all harms— these constitute the three increases of the elements.
Diligence regarding all phenomena and the mental application of meditative concentration;
Constantly practicing wisdom, one further increases the attainment of bodhi.
Skillful means act in concert with wisdom, and through vows, all are rendered pure;
by means of the powers and the wondrous, firm knowledge, the elements increase into four kinds.
"To not pay homage to a bodhisattva is an extremely evil teaching;
by not associating with a bodhisattva, one does not give rise to the Dharma-body.
It is like wishing to eat rock candy while increasing the planting of sugarcane."
If the sugarcane seed is destroyed, there is no way for granulated sugar to arise.
If the sugarcane seed is protected, three kinds may be obtained:
coarse sugar, half-sugar, and granulated sugar; among these, it will certainly be produced.
If one protects the bodhicitta, three types may be attained:
Arhat, Pratyekabuddha, or Buddha; among these, one will certainly be born.
Just as a farmer must protect the rice sprouts,
so the Tathāgata will surely provide protection for those who possess initial resolute practice.
Just as on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, one beholds the form of the lunar disc;
In this way, through the practice of resolute conviction, the form and marks of a Buddha appear as reflections.
Just as the initial lunar disc increases moment by moment,
so too does the one who has entered the stages perceive an increase in realization in every thought-moment.
Just as on the fifteenth day of the waxing moon, the lunar disk becomes perfectly full;
so too, upon the ultimate stage, the Dharmakāya is brought to birth.
One’s resolute conviction regarding the Buddha’s Dharma should always remain firm.
One who can give rise to such a mind attains the state of non-retrogression.
When the basis of defilement is transformed into the transformation of the basis, one attains it as the pure basis;
through partial awakening, this is called the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
Constantly regarding the various defilements such as desire within the state of affliction, one attains purity free from stain;
this is called the Ground of Freedom from Stain (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
Having destroyed the net of afflictions, one shines forth, having attained freedom from stain.
The immeasurable darkness of ignorance is dispelled; this is called the Ground of Radiance.
Constantly pure and luminous, far removed from worldly auspiciousness, and surrounded by the flames of wisdom, it is named the Ground of Blazing Wisdom.
All arts and crafts, adorned with various meditative concentrations;
difficult to conquer the afflictions, they attain the ground Difficult to Conquer (Abhimukhī).
Regarding the three types of enlightenment, they embrace them and bring them to fulfillment.
The profound arising and ceasing is named the Ground of Presence;
Sporting within the net of light, universally adorned by Śakra,
Transcending the torrential flood of desire is named the Ground of Far-Going.
Empowered by all Buddhas, they enter the ocean of wisdom;
possessing mastery and effortlessness, they remain unmoved by the emissaries of Māra.
Regarding the analytical knowledges, they have reached the further shore through yoga.
In the discourse and discussion of the Dharma, it is called the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (Sādhumatī).
The body is accomplished through wisdom, stainless like space;
sustained by all Buddhas, it is as pervasive as the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā).
The basis upon which the Buddha-dharma relies, wherein both practice and its fruit are sustained;
because that which is relied upon is entirely transformed, it is called the Dharma-body.
It is free from inconceivable perfuming and free from the habit-energies of transmigration.
If you think that there is a thinker, how can such a thing be known?
It transcends all realms of speech and is not an object for any of the sense faculties.
That which is grasped by the mental consciousness is like the nature of the self as it truly is.
Accumulating them in successive order, the sons of the Buddha with great renown,
through the wisdom of the Dharma-clouds, perceive the subtle nature of phenomena.
At that time, they cleanse their minds and cross over the ocean of birth and death.
He established a great lotus flower as his grand seat;
its immeasurable jewel-petals radiated light, and its pedestal was composed of precious brilliance.
Immeasurable billions of lotus flowers served as its surrounding retinue.
First, by means of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the remaining unique qualities of a Buddha, he sits in great sovereignty.
All virtues are gathered therein; merit and wisdom serve as his provisions.
As the full moon dwells among the constellations, surrounded by them on all sides;
so with the hand of the Buddha-sun, using stainless jewel-light,
he consecrates the eldest son, causing him to be consecrated everywhere.
Abiding in the Great Yoga, they all see with the divine eye:
how the world is agitated by ignorance, beset by evil habits, suffering, and fear.
Appearing like the color of golden light, it issues forth from that yogic radiance.
Enveloped by ignorance, they now open the gate of nescience.
Through the invocation of merit and wisdom, they attain the samādhi of non-attachment;
following conditions toward parinirvāṇa, their minds achieve total transformation.
All phenomena lack intrinsic nature; as for that intrinsic nature within the objective realm, the Bodhisattva King perceives it wondrously: the Dharma-body is wondrously stainless.
With these entirely stainless bodies, they dwell securely in the ocean of wisdom.
Thus performing benefit for sentient beings, like a skillful maṇi jewel;
all practitioners of yoga, masters of Mahāyoga;
the reflections of the Buddha, entirely transformed, pervade and flow forth everywhere.
Some have eight arms, with three eyes and a blazing body;
they are all kings of yoga, emanating everywhere.
With hands of compassion, they joyfully hold the bow of supreme bliss.
Shooting with the arrow of Prajñā, one severs all subtle ignorance.
Advancing with great power, one grasps the staff of wisdom;
the shells of all ignorance are shattered everywhere.
Powerful sentient beings, with bodies blazing like vajras,
act as Vajrapāṇi for the sake of subduing sentient beings;
those who perform actions for themselves manifest various fruits.
Instructing according to the principles of the Dharma, he becomes the King of Equanimity;
to those whose bodies are tormented by the fierce fires of hunger and thirst, he is able to bestow all manner of food and drink;
and to those who constantly suffer from various ailments, he is a skilled king of physicians.
The Māra-king among his retinue, the māras’ daughters in their finery;
the Bodhisattva acts as their kinsman, able to bestow the site of enlightenment.
Like the forms of the sun and moon, their radiance is entirely pleasing to the mind.
The radiance flows forth like flashes of lightning, illuminating billions of lands.
Because of a single lamp, all are universally illuminated and set ablaze;
yet if that one lamp is extinguished, everything follows it to extinction.
Thus, the Buddha of Maturation manifests various kinds of light;
one manifests nirvāṇa, while other Buddhas demonstrate the entry into peace.
Yet even this one does not undergo extinction—how could the light of the sun ever produce darkness?
Constantly manifesting appearance and disappearance, you reveal oceans of buddha-fields.
In this world shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, you are able to purify the eye of wisdom;
traveling to millions of lands, you compassionately transform sentient beings.
They are all free from weariness, due to the armor of their great compassion;
they have reached the further shore of all supernormal powers through yoga.
Observing both the opportune and the inopportune moments, they cause beings to flow along [the path].
Firm against flattery and crookedness, one abandons them for a moment.
To tame immeasurable sentient beings, one suddenly brings them to purification;
through the transformations of immeasurable Buddhas, one instantly attains temporary transformation.
Within the ocean of the three realms, they cast the net of subduing;
they unfurl the wondrous net of the Dharma to bring all beings everywhere to maturity.
Thus, by means of the net of subduing, they cause all to reach full maturity.
Universally causing those who drift within it to be raised up—
just as if one had universally delivered a thousand sentient beings;
having delivered them, causing them to awaken to the sublime Dharma without doubt.
The World-Honored One’s bell of the wondrous Dharma causes all to hear it universally;
by virtue of this vibrating sound, the dust of afflictions is cast away.
Those with excessive ignorance are purified in a single moment.
By the majestic power of the sun’s radiance, may all veils and obscurations be destroyed.
For those who follow after the afflictions of darkness and other sinful beings,
may they be brought to benefit and gradually purified.
To each person he manifests an emanation, dwelling peacefully like the moon in water;
yet those whose minds are agitated by afflictions do not see the Tathāgata,
just as hungry ghosts perceive the ocean everywhere as parched dryness.
Thus, for one with little merit, there is no Buddha to perform the act of discernment.
How could the Tathāgata act for a sentient being with little merit?
It would be like placing the most supreme jewel into the hand of one born blind.
How can one behold the unsurpassed Dharma-body,
With a body like ten million suns, Enveloped by a net of light?
Even the devas, with their meager merit, Are unable to see it.
Regarding the Great God (Mahādeva) mentioned previously: how can he be seen?
His form cannot be perceived, for the sages are free from afflictions;
as for the gods, asuras, Brahmās, and others—how could they possess even a modicum of wisdom?
Yet, through the Buddha’s majestic power and because of the purity of one's own mind,
one is able to see such forms as these and obtain all prosperity.
When sentient beings possess the dignity of merit, the Buddha dwells before those people.
His body shines with radiance, Adorned with the thirty-two supreme marks.
Such a Great Being as this Should be seen as being like the great ocean;
Before long, he will attain Wisdom that is like the ocean.
World-Honored One, that physical body dwells securely through many eons;
it is able to tame those who can be tamed for their benefit and leads them toward the categories of ethical discipline.
If [this] Great Yoga possesses such vast longevity, by what cause does [the other] have short life?
To many beings numbering more than a koṭi, he manifests the increase or decrease of lifespan;
for immeasurable koṭis of kalpas, he extends his life-force.
Because all causes and conditions are inexhaustible, he attains the fruit of inexhaustibility.
If there is a corresponding [teaching] that reveals this principle, one should analyze it with wisdom using only the body;
such a person will be born within a pure lotus flower, hearing the Dharma spoken of Amitāyus.
The Praise of the Dharmakāya as Requested by Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva from the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, Recited One Hundred Thousand Times.
